This expansion is coupled with the company’s recent purchase of approximately 2,500 acres from the provincial land bank, which sextupled the company’s footprint to about 3,000 acres. “Securing this initial $120 million in new contracts and investment is a turning point for HFI,” said Rhiannon Iles, president of HFI Pyrotechnics. “The Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal’s land bank, completed this past April, made the land available for us to grow, and we are investing to develop it with new buildings, equipment, and utilities. Photo by John Lawless / The Brockville Recorder and Times HFI celebrated this milestone with a groundbreaking event Thursday morning, attended by local dignitaries such as MP Michael Barrett, MPP Steve Clark and Edwardsburgh Cardinal Mayor Tory Deschamps. The groundbreaking signified the beginning of the construction of a new laboratory for quality assurance, which aims to help with innovation and research and development. “This expansion is incredibly important to our council, not only because it brings high-quality, good-paying jobs to our community, but because it transforms lands that sat unproductive for far too long into a hub of opportunity,” said Deschamps. “We are proud to support HFI’s continued success and look forward to the long-term benefits this and other future projects will bring to Edwardsburgh Cardinal.” Read More Prescott-area company helped Artemis II return to Earth HFI Pyrotechnics buys large parcel from provincial land bank HFI said the $120-million investment is the first phase of a five-year growth plan, with more expansion news to follow. Article content Over the next one to two years, HFI will invest in new buildings, civil work, and heavy equipment across the site. That work includes the land bank acquisition; a major project on the production floor to increase capacity for marine location markers with new industrial equipment to raise output; hydro and bandwidth upgrades; and, construction across the site that will include new buildings, access roads, and supporting infrastructure. The investment will bring new contracts, new infrastructure, and new research programs to the site, which will equate to work that is already creating jobs at one of the largest employers in Leeds and Grenville. The company has added 50 positions since November and expects to add more through the rest of this year as production grows. “When I started in 2020 there were 57 employees, and now including the expansion in November, we’re over 150,” said Iles. “In that time, we’ve built some great relationships with the U.S. and some of our other NATO partners. We have shipments going out to Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland all in the next month or so. “But Canada is our No.-1 customer and our most important customer.” HFI designs, manufactures, and supplies specialty pyrotechnic products for military, defence, and commercial customers worldwide. Its products help train and protect armed forces and support search-and-rescue and safety operations. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian Gambling Former Liberal MP condemns Coalition for backing gambling reforms that ‘let down’ vulnerable Australians Jenny Ware, member of inquiry that recommended wagering advertising ban, says ‘public health crisis’ demands stronger response from major parties Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.12 EDT Last modified on Fri 21 Aug 2026 00.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The former Liberal MP Jenny Ware has condemned her one-time Coalition colleagues for backing Labor’s gambling legislation, claiming “vulnerable Australians have been let down”, as the parliament failed to back a full ban on wagering ads. Ware, a member of the Peta Murphy-led inquiry in 2023 that recommended entirely ending wagering advertising and inducements, called gambling a public health crisis that demanded a much stronger response from both sides of politics. “Vulnerable Australians deserve better than political convenience dressed up as consensus,” she told Guardian Australia. “Australians deserve better on gambling reform that should meet the scale of the harm.” Labor’s gambling reforms passed parliament on Wednesday night. Described by the government as the strongest wagering legislation ever enacted, TV ads will be limited to three an hour between 5am and 8.30pm, online ads will only be shown to those over 18 and with a mandatory opt-out option, advertising on players’ jerseys and sporting stadiums will eventually be banned, and there will be new restrictions on inducements, celebrity endorsements and employee commissions from gambling losses. Australians could soon be able to block all online gambling ads. But will the plan actually work? Read more But there are questions over how a new “opt-out register” will work , with sources in the wagering, tech and media industries saying they were blind-sided by that announcement, which only came on Monday. Wagering operators – who are obliged to pay for the register’s development – have said they are anxious to know how the website will be developed, and how much they will have to pay. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and the communications minister, Anika Wells, said the reforms aimed to protect the most vulnerable from harm while balancing the rights of Australians to gamble if they wished. The government decided not to impose a full ban on online gambling ads and inducements, as Murphy – the late Labor MP who died in 2023 – had recommended in her report. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Ware, a member of Murphy’s committee, said the parliament – and her former Coalition colleagues – should have done more, saying “the full suite” of Murphy’s recommendations should have been enacted, including a national gambling regulator and a full ad ban. Murphy’s husband, Rod Glover , also spoke this week of his “mixed emotions” at the legislation’s passage , praising some reforms but saying it was “far from everything that is needed”. Ware said: “The legislation that passed this week falls far short of the report’s recommendations. “Gambling harm is a national public health crisis hiding in plain sight. The government lacks the morality and political courage that Australians expect on this.” She praised a handful of her former Coalition colleagues, including Andrew Wallace and Pat Conaghan, who had crossed the floor to vote against the legislation and called for more action, and said some amendments pursued by cross-benchers should have been taken up. “It is deeply disappointing that the federal opposition voted with the government to block stronger, evidence-based protections led by cross-benchers,” Ware said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “I met personally with families who had lost loved ones to gambling-related suicide – families the prime minister declined to meet. Their stories were heartbreaking and courageous, and they deserve more than partial reform pushed through for political expediency by the major parties.” 'What's the point?' asks Nationals MP during fiery speech on gambling reforms – video Albanese on the ABC’s 7.30 said he believed Labor had “got the balance right” on its reforms. “We have worked constructively with the entire sector, including I’ve sat down with the people who are part of the anti-gambling industry, sat down with sporting organisations. I haven’t sat down with the betting industry. But I’ve sat down with others, including, of course, the free-to-air networks who have arrangements in place,” he said. “I think it’s very positive reform, whilst acknowledging that the problem isn’t someone having a bet on a Saturday if that’s what they do.” Wells on Friday marked three years of the BetStop self-exclusion register, which she said had seen 67,000 total registrations and 41,000 currently on the register. Nearly 80% of all registrations were people aged under 40, and 38% had registered for a lifetime ban from access to gambling operators. This week’s legislation includes moves to strengthen BetStop, including obligating gambling providers to fund an awareness campaign for the service. “BetStop has already made such a huge difference to so many Australians – that’s why we’re taking steps to make it even stronger and more effective and working to raise awareness of this vital service,” Wells said. https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article.text: Return to Homepage Top Stories: Weird weather Milo Yiannopoulos deported U.S. - Venezuela oil deal Freedom Fuel laswuit Lake Ontario renaming Trump's noncitizen vote claims Mail-in voting Near-total lunar eclipse Tropical Storm Dolly CIA director's Moscow visit Investing.com -- A Spanish F/A-18 fighter jet operating under NATO's air-policing mission shot down a drone that entered Romanian airspace without authorisation early on Sunday, Reuters reported, citing Romania's defence ministry. The drone was detected entering Romania from neighbouring Moldova, about 24 kilometres north of the southeastern city of Galați. The ministry did not identify the aircraft's origin. Advertisement Advertisement The Spanish fighter established radar contact with the drone and received permission to engage it before shooting it down safely at 5:01 a.m. local time, according to the statement. Fragments from the aircraft appeared to have landed in an uninhabited area between two villages. Officials did not report any injuries or property damage. The incident marked the fourth drone Romania has shot down this year amid repeated incursions linked to Russia's attacks on neighbouring Ukraine. Romania shares a 614-kilometre border with Ukraine and is a member of NATO. Russian drones have repeatedly entered its airspace during more than four years of war. Advertisement Advertisement Romanian authorities have also encountered drifting mines in the Black Sea, raising security concerns around important energy and commercial shipping routes. In July, Romanian F-16 pilots shot down three Russian drones that breached the country's airspace. Those were the first such interceptions after dozens of reported incursions since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Earlier in 2026, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați during an overnight attack on targets across the border in Ukraine. Two people were injured in that incident. Sunday's interception points to the continued risk that Russian attacks near NATO's eastern border could spill into allied territory, requiring aircraft stationed under the bloc's air-policing mission to respond. Photograph: Alexander Kazakov/Sputnik/Kremlin via AP Donald Trump ‘We hope he’ll accept’: US invites Putin to G20 summit at Trump golf club Kremlin yet to respond publicly to US invitation that is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and EU countries Andrew Roth in New York Wed 23 Sep 2026 14.09 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 16.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The United States has invited Vladimir Putin to take part in the meeting of the G20 scheduled in Miami in December in what would be the first major summit with the Russian leader present since he launched his invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The invitation, which marks a significant reversal by the Trump administration of Russia’s international isolation, was announced by Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, during a press conference on the sidelines of the United Nations conference in New York. “We’ve invited President Putin to the G20,” Rubio said in a televised press conference following a meeting with Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov. “We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with [Trump] but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept.” Iran’s president says his country’s people have been ‘victims of terrorism’ by the United States - live Read more The Kremlin has not yet responded publicly to the invitation, which is likely to raise concerns from Ukraine and other European leaders who have recently accused Russia of launching hybrid attacks to disrupt logistics and spread political uncertainty among Kyiv’s allies. Russia remains a member of the G20 but Putin has not attended a summit of the body since 2019. He did attend one session virtually in 2023. The December summit is set to take place at the Trump National Doral golf club. Rubio framed the invitation by saying that Trump was willing to meet with “virtually anyone” and that “in order to solve problems, you have to meet with people you disagree with”. He said Trump remained open to meeting with Putin one-on-one in other forums, if “there’s a purpose behind the meeting”. The G20 is a forum of the world’s largest economies and includes the European Union, China, India, the United States, the United Kingdom, and other major countries. European officials were upset by a decision to invite Russian finance minister Anton Siluanov to a meeting of the group’s top economic officials in August and refused to pose in a “family photo” with him at the summit. Zelenskyy had said earlier this month that he would be ready to travel to the summit and would meet with Putin if he attended. “We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions,” he told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle in an interview. “It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That’s it.” On Wednesday, Zelenskyy addressed the United Nations, urging world leaders to keep choking Russia’s revenues and impede its war effort. “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us,” said Zelenskyy. “In response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.” Zelenskyy also warned that the war could spread beyond Ukraine if Putin was not stopped. Rubio on Wednesday also indicated that he had spoken with Lavrov about the accusations of “hybrid attacks” in Europe, saying that one concern about the war was that “it could metastasize and spread into other places”. Trump is currently seeking to negotiate a partial ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that would include attacks on Russian oil refineries in order to take pressure off global energy prices. In particular, Trump has called on Zelenskyy to halt attacks against Russian oil in order to reduce prices on diesel fuel, which have spiked to almost double their price last year in the United States before midterm elections for Congress. Trump and Zelenskyy met on the sidelines of the United Nations on Tuesday for a rare face-to-face discussion of measures to end the war. Zelenskyy called for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Putin to end the war, but the Kremlin has declined past attempts for direct meetings with Zelenskyy. “President Trump, our teams, and I spoke about how to end the war. This is the priority. We are ready. I’m not sure Russia is ready as of today, but anyhow, we spoke about an energy ceasefire,” Zelenskyy said on Tuesday. Despite efforts to broker a ceasefire, however, Russia has continued to pummel Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities with drone and missile attacks. Kyiv hit a major Russian oil refinery over the weekend in its largest attack on Russia’s capital yet. ‘The choice was prison or exile’: journalists who fled Russia publish grim portrait of Putin Read more For the past two days, Kyiv has come under particularly severe attack from jet-powered Shahed drones – swifter and harder to intercept than their predecessors. As has been the case since mid-August, the drone attacks have come in the daytime as well as at night, disrupting ordinary life, schools and kindergartens. On Wednesday morning an acrid stench of burning filled the city centre after multiple explosions, and the clear autumnal sky was clouded with plumes of black smoke. A petrol station, warehouses, a business centre and a transport infrastructure building were hit, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. As of mid-morning, one person had died and eight had been injured. Explosions were seen near the capital’s main railway station. Congress last week passed a sweeping sanctions bill against Russia that would also give Trump the authority to levy 100% tariffs against top purchasers of Russian energy exports, including China and India. Democrats, who mostly opposed the bill, said that it gave Trump too much power to levy tariffs and that they could be used against US allies as well. In response to what has happened, the House foreign affairs committee posted on X : “Trump signed the Russia sanctions bill 5 days ago. Today Rubio makes clear the administration has no intention of isolating Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.” Charlotte Higgins contributed reporting from Kyiv Explore more on these topics Donald Trump Vladimir Putin US politics US foreign policy G20 Miami Florida news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/tate-brot.text: Jessica Coates Fri, September 18, 2026 at 2:01 AM UTC 0 UK lawyers for Andrew and Tristan Tate said they plan to challenge a bid to extradite the brothers from the US to Britain through a judicial review. British prosecutors earlier this month lodged a formal request with the US State Department to bring the social media influencers back to the UK to face rape and sex trafficking charges. Speaking to Piers Morgan on Thursday night, Andrew Ford and Adam Rasul of defence solicitors Holborn Adams argued the brothers should first face separate criminal proceedings in Romania . Both men deny any wrongdoing. Mr Ford said: “We have started a process of judicial review to challenge the UK’s decision to seek extradition. “In March 2024, Romania made an order to agree to extradition back to the UK, but once Romanian proceedings are concluded.” Mr Ford argued pursuing UK extradition while proceedings in Romania remained ongoing would “deprive them of their opportunity to be exonerated”, adding it would “impact upon their ability to be able to defend themselves in the UK”. The judicial review allows a court to examine whether a decision by a public body was made lawfully. The US State Department is reviewing the UK’s extradition applications to ensure they comply with the existing treaty between London and Washington. Once this process has been completed, the applications will be sent to the US Justice Department , which will forward them to the court to make the final decision on the extradition request. An official letter from the State Department details that Andrew Tate , 39, is “wanted to stand trial in the United Kingdom” on a series of charges, including 10 counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm. He is also accused of making and distributing indecent images of a child and possessing extreme pornography. Charges levelled against Tristan Tate, 38, include five counts of rape, six counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, three counts of sex trafficking and a sexual assault. The brothers’ US lawyer, Joe McBride, said he would be challenging the requests, arguing they were not backed up by the information needed under the provisions of the extradition agreement between the UK and the US. Romanian authorities earlier this month charged Andrew Tate with complicity in trafficking a minor and money laundering, while Tristan Tate was indicted for complicity in trafficking in minors and money laundering. https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-c.text: Six weeks after the EU unveiled its much-anticipated proposal to protect kids across the bloc from social media, European governments are pressing ahead with their own rules. National political leaders had spent months asking for unified age restrictions for social media access across the European Union, to avoid 27 different sets of rules. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s response came in September with the EU Kids Act, a signature initiative of her second term that would ban under-13s from accessing most current social media platforms and severely restrict access for under-15s. But it is becoming clear that individual countries don’t want to wait for the Brussels legislative wheels to turn — and in some cases, are proceeding with national laws that would kick even more kids off the platforms than what von der Leyen has in mind. Advertisement Advertisement “While we wait for the EU Kids Act – we are pushing forward with national legislation,” Denmark’s digital minister Christina Egelund said. “The problems are urgent. Children and parents should not be asked to wait.” Last week, Greece’s parliament passed a bill to bar social media access for under-15s, while Italy’s own stalled efforts to shield under-14s suddenly found new winds . By Thursday, the Commission will have to give the first indication of how it will deal with national laws. Its response to Austria’s proposal to bar social media access for under-14s will be the first test case. Capitals continue to ultimately favor a unified EU law, which is in line with existing rules that give Brussels oversight of big platforms like Instagram and TikTok. A harmonized law also avoids fragmenting the market with different rules in different countries. Yet agreeing on a final text for the legislation and implementing the Kids Act will take more than a year — too long for national leaders eager to show they are serious about protecting the mental health of kids and reining in Big Tech. The age at which limits are set is also a sticking point, with countries preferring various thresholds between 13 and 16. “Greece decided to move forward with its own legislation on minors’ access to social media because protecting children is a pressing issue that calls for timely and concrete action,” a spokesperson for the country's digital ministry said. “We have a responsibility to address an issue that is already affecting the daily lives of children and their families," they said, adding that the Greek law is “complementary” to the EU’s and that Athens is still in favor of a bloc-wide solution. Advertisement Advertisement Portugal formally notified the Commission of its own law a little over a week after the Kids Act was proposed, formally asking the EU executive to say if Lisbon’s plans are in line with European rules. Cyprus’s ministers approved their own ban for under-15s on the day Brussels proposed its law. Austria and Germany have also not shown any signs of slowing down. Many of these countries had backed an EU-wide solution. The current trajectory could create a confusing situation for minors, who may find themselves locked out of social media in January 2027 only to then regain access under parental controls once the Kids Act is implemented later that year or in 2028. The Commission had stressed that the law would bring about “maximum harmonization,” meaning national laws would be scrapped if and when the EU-wide measures came into force. The Kids Act will have to be negotiated between the European Commission, European Parliament and EU governments. | Carl Court/Getty Images When France first formally informed the Commission of its national law to ban social media access for under-15s, “we said very clearly: you should be able, and you should be ready to repeal this law once there are European measures in place,” a senior Commission official told reporters when announcing the law in September. But a few weeks later, Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told POLITICO that the EU executive was still considering how to respond to the laws that have been submitted to be checked for compatibility with European rules. The Kids Act will have to be negotiated between the Commission, the European Parliament and EU governments, meaning it may not be finalized for months. It would then come into force six months later. The senior official estimated negotiations would take eight to 12 months starting next September, putting the implementation date well into 2028.
